<section id="overview" class="content-section">

## What is Jason Rau Ankle Lock System?

**The Jason Rau Ankle Lock System is a BJJGraph study framework for connecting ankle-lock control with the positional decisions created by a defender's changing posture.**

Dynamic Ankle Locks provides a specific course companion for studying grips and leg position alongside seated, kneeling and standing reactions. Its syllabus extends beyond straight ankle locks to other submissions and back-take options. That distinction matters when choosing a section for a particular training session.

The plan below is BJJGraph's original study sequence. It begins with recognising whether the ankle and leg remain connected to the attacker as the defender changes posture. A lost connection can make a positional transition more sensible than continuing the original submission. Select permitted techniques with a coach, and keep advanced Aoki-lock or heel-hook branches separate from a straight-ankle-only practice objective.

</section>

<section id="key-principles" class="content-section">

## Core Principles
- Assess the leg connection as well as the hand grip.
- Name whether the defender is seated, kneeling or standing before choosing a response.
- Treat a posture change as a new control problem rather than a reason to squeeze harder.
- Distinguish straight ankle locks from other submissions in the course.
- Keep back-take options available when the original leg connection is no longer useful.
- Define allowed attacks before an entanglement round begins.


</section>

<section id="key-components" class="content-section">

## Key Components
**Grip and leg-position pairing** (Identify whether the whole position supports the attempted attack.)
Compare the selected ankle grip with the leg arrangement supporting it rather than evaluating either in isolation.

**Posture classification** (Choose the relevant lesson for the actual exchange.)
Observe the different balance and connection problems presented by a seated, kneeling or standing defender.

**Connection-loss response** (Avoid chasing the original finish after its positional basis is gone.)
Notice when the attacker can no longer maintain useful leg contact despite retaining the foot with the hands.

**Secondary-route selection** (Make the next objective explicit instead of switching locks blindly.)
Compare guard recovery or a coached back-take route with a permitted secondary submission.



</section>

<section id="implementation-sequence" class="content-section">

## Implementation Sequence
1. **Choose one straight-ankle position**: Begin in a familiar leg entanglement and identify the grip and leg contact used in the selected lesson.


2. **Test seated posture**: Let the partner make one small seated adjustment. Stop when either the grip or supporting leg connection ceases to control the exchange.


3. **Compare a kneeling reaction**: Use the corresponding course section to review what changes when the partner comes to their knees. Keep the entry task free of finishing pressure.


4. **Name the loss of connection**: Rehearse a deliberate release or positional fallback when the legs can no longer support the original attack.


5. **Add one secondary route**: Select a coach-approved back-take or other permitted branch. Compare its required control with the option of recovering guard.




</section>

<section id="common-obstacles" class="content-section hide-minimal">

## What Challenges Will You Face?
- **The hands retain the foot while the legs lose contact.**: Stop and diagnose the leg-position problem instead of increasing finishing effort.
- **The same answer is used against every defender posture.**: Separate seated and kneeling rounds and identify the different control requirements.
- **A straight-ankle drill drifts into another leg lock.**: Name permitted attacks in advance and reset before an unagreed branch.
- **A back take is assumed whenever the ankle lock fails.**: Check that the new route has its own connection and choose guard recovery when it does not.


</section>

<section id="assessment-metrics" class="content-section">

## How to Measure Your Progress
**Connection assessment**: Observe whether the grip and leg position work together.
Proficiency indicators:
- Identifies supporting contact
- Recognises a hand-only hold
- Can release deliberately


**Posture recognition**: Classify the defender's posture before selecting a response.
Proficiency indicators:
- Distinguishes seated from kneeling
- Recognises a standing change
- Chooses a relevant study section


**Branch boundaries**: Check that the drill remains within its agreed submission scope.
Proficiency indicators:
- Names allowed locks
- Recognises a different branch
- Resets before an unagreed attack


**Fallback quality**: Review the next objective after losing ankle-lock control.
Proficiency indicators:
- Can recover guard
- Can describe a back-take requirement
- Declines an unsupported transition




</section>

<section id="training-methodology" class="content-section hide-minimal">

## How to Train This System Effectively

### Drilling Approach
BJJGraph suggests two entry-and-control rounds from the same ankle-lock position: one with the partner seated and one with a slow kneeling reaction. Keep finishing pressure out of the comparison. Record whether the first loss is the hand grip or supporting leg contact, then use that observation to select a course lesson and a coached fallback.

### Progression Path
**Pairing** (Focus: Recognise the relationship between the ankle grip and supporting leg position.)
**Posture** (Focus: Compare seated and kneeling defensive reactions.)
**Disconnection** (Focus: Practise deliberate release and guard recovery.)
**Branching** (Focus: Add one permitted secondary route with clear control requirements.)


### Common Mistakes
- Holding the foot after the rest of the entanglement has disappeared.
- Treating all ankle-related submissions as interchangeable.
- Forcing a back take without establishing its entry connection.


</section>
